Kallar Kahar, Salt Range

About me

A leadership story rooted in place

I grew up between small towns and salt hills in Pakistan, and I learned early that the people around you are what make a place liveable. That belief shapes everything I do: the study circles I run, the students I mentor, the sessions I facilitate, and the essays I write.

Over the past three years I have mentored junior and female engineering students, taught digital skills to learners from underserved backgrounds, coordinated student events, and helped hundreds of new students feel less alone in their first weeks at university. I am most fulfilled when someone leaves a conversation feeling heard, supported, and more confident in their own ability.

I am particularly committed to women's leadership, inclusive education, community building, and learning across cultures. Technology is part of my training, but people are my subject.

Leadership philosophy

Listen, include, teach, connect, empower

Not a single big event, but small, repeated habits: showing up every week, noticing who is missing, and making it possible for them to come.

Noticing who is missing from the room, and asking them what they need before building anything.

Lead from beside, not above.

The best mentoring sessions feel like sitting next to someone, not standing over them.

Build small, repeat often.

A weekly study circle changes more lives than a one-time event.

Leave it stronger than you found it.

If a group can’t survive without me, I haven’t led. I’ve just been present.

Women & leadership

Making room for women in engineering

"When a woman in a lecture hall of ninety men sees one other woman lead, the room changes shape."

Mentoring female engineering students

Ongoing one-to-one and small-group mentoring for 15+ women in my department, covering coursework, confidence, and next steps after graduation.

Honest conversations about STEM

Creating space where women can name the challenges they face — being spoken over, doubted, or isolated — and think through them together.

Confidence and leadership

Encouraging women to take visible roles: presenting, leading study circles, coordinating events, and mentoring the year below them.

Supportive peer-learning spaces

Building study and discussion groups where mutual support, inclusion, and women's participation are the default, not the exception.

Related learning: YALI Network — Legal Barriers to Women's Rights · Skills for Prosperity — Safeguarding, Economic Inclusion & Gender Equality · Women in Leadership Webinar Series.

A moment of failure and growth

Three people showed up

In my first year of mentoring, I assumed students would come if I built the space. I almost cancelled the second session. Instead, I asked them what they needed.

3 people in the room

Leadership is not about building a stage. It is listening first and building second. Every initiative since has started with one question: who isn’t in this room, and why?

Writing & literary work

Landscape, memory, belonging

Poem · Nature · 2026

The Lake at Dusk

The surface of a childhood lake becomes a place where memory, distance, and the passage of time meet.
The light goes down the way it always has, unhurried, unconcerned with who is watching— gold folding into grey along the water, the hills drawing their old blue line behind it. I have been gone longer than I lived here, and still the lake does not ask where. It keeps the shape of the evening the way a hand keeps the shape of a bowl. Somewhere a boy is throwing stones that will never reach the far shore. I was that boy. I am still counting the rings before they disappear. Nothing here has changed enough to notice, which is its own kind of mercy— a place that stayed still so I would have somewhere to come back to.
Poem · Landscape · 2025

Salt in the Hills

A meditation on the Salt Range, exploring the relationship between landscape, history, and the marks left by time.
The hills do not remember names, only weight— the weight of feet, of carts, of centuries pressed into whatever passes for soil. Salt rises through the rock like a memory that refuses to be buried, white veins in the red evening, a mineral patience older than any of us. Wind moves through the passes the way it must have moved before there were roads to follow it, before anyone thought to name the wind. I walk here and feel small in the correct proportion— not erased, only reminded that the hills were keeping time before I arrived to ask what time it was.
Poem · Nature · 2025

Before the Streetlights

A recollection of nights when the sky belonged to darkness, stars, and the quietness of an earlier world.
Before the streetlights, the sky came all the way down. We didn't know to call it light pollution— we called it a good night, one with enough stars to lose count on purpose. My grandmother would sit outside past dark, not doing anything, which felt like doing everything. The night had room in it then for silence that wasn't waiting to be filled. Now the sky over that same yard holds maybe a dozen stars, apologetically, between the glow of somebody's porch light and the glow of somebody's screen. I don't say this to complain about progress. I say it because I was there before the light got so loud it drowned out the quiet, ordinary dark.
Poem · Memory · 2025

A Mountain Seen Once

A brief glimpse of a distant mountain becomes an enduring image, questioning why certain moments remain with us.
It was there for the length of a curve in the road, grey-blue, unnamed, gone before the bus finished the turn that revealed it— and somehow it has outlasted places I lived in for years. I don't remember the town before it or the town after. I remember the mountain the way you remember a name you were never told. Maybe permanence isn't about time spent but about the angle of the light when a thing chooses to be seen. The mountain didn't ask to be remembered. It just was, once, entirely. I have visited grander places since, stood in front of things built to be looked at. None of them have followed me home the way that mountain did, uninvited, unbothered, still there.
Poem · Nature · 2024

What the River Keeps

A reflection on rivers as witnesses to generations, carrying fragments of memory long after people have moved on.
The river doesn't keep names either, but it keeps something— the bend where a boat once turned, the bank where a house used to stand before the house left. People move the way water insists on moving: downstream, away, toward somewhere else, while the river stays in place by the simple trick of never stopping. I used to think it forgot everything, carried it out to some larger, indifferent sea. Now I think it keeps a kind of ledger— silt is just memory that settled. Whatever we can't carry with us, the river takes without complaint, holding what our leaving couldn't, and letting the rest run on toward the wide, forgetting sea.
Poem · Family · 2024

The Tree Outside My Grandfather's House

Childhood memories gather around an old tree as a family home slowly disappears into the past.
The tree is taller than the house now, which the house does not seem to mind. It has watched the paint change twice, the door change once, and still hasn't finished growing. I carved nothing into it as a child— I was told not to, and, for once, I listened. It didn't need my initials. It already knew whose hands had climbed it. My grandfather used to sit beneath it in the hour before the heat set in, as if the shade itself were a kind of company that didn't require conversation. The house will likely be sold someday, the way houses are, when the people who filled them have gone on to fill other rooms. The tree, I think, will simply keep standing— the last relative who never had to leave.
Poem · Landscape · 2024

After the Rain

A familiar landscape is transformed by rain, revealing how places can change while still holding their memories.
The street I've walked a thousand times looks unfamiliar for exactly one hour after rain— the dust gone, the color returned to things that had quietly agreed to fade. Even the hills seem to reconsider themselves, sharper at the edges, closer than they were, as if the rain had washed away some agreed-upon distance between us and them. I like this hour because it lies a little— it suggests the place could always look like this, freshly made, uncomplicated, before the dust remembers its job and returns. By evening the ordinary version comes back, and I am glad of it too. Change, even brief, is proof that the place was never as fixed as I assumed.
Poem · Nature · 2023

The Last Quiet Field

A quiet reflection on rural spaces disappearing beneath roads, buildings, and the movement of modern life.
There is one field left that no one has built on, mostly because no one has gotten around to it yet. I go there when I want to remember what the whole valley used to sound like. Nothing dramatic happens in a quiet field. That is, in fact, the entire point of it. Grass moves. A bird decides something. The silence isn't empty—it's simply not for sale. I know what's coming. I've watched it happen to every field before this one— the stakes, the noise, the sudden certainty that quiet was only ever a waiting room. So I go now, before the waiting ends, and stand in what's left of the nothing, trying to memorize a sound that no one will think to record until it's gone.
Poem · Belonging · 2023

Maps of Home

An exploration of home as something carried within us, shaped by places, people, language, and memory.
Home was never only the house— it was the specific slant of afternoon light across a particular wall, a language spoken nowhere else exactly like this. I have left it more than once and found, each time, that I hadn't— that a map of it had folded itself into some drawer I keep carrying. You can leave the streets. You cannot leave the sound of your name said in the voice that first taught you to answer to it. That part of the map has no edges. So when people ask where I'm from, I give them the province, the district, the town— useful, but incomplete, a shorthand for something I keep no other copy of.
Poem · Memory · 2023

Night Without Electricity

A childhood night without electricity opens into a world of stars, conversation, silence, and unexpected closeness.
The night the power failed, no one panicked. Someone found a candle. Someone found a story. My uncle, who never talked much, suddenly had opinions about everything. Outside, the stars did what they always do when nothing competes with them— they simply became visible again, patient, as if they'd been waiting for an opening. We sat in the courtyard longer than we meant to, past the hour we'd normally have scattered to separate rooms and separate screens, because there was, for once, nowhere else worth going. When the lights came back, something in the room changed— not sadly, just quietly, the way a conversation ends when it has, without announcement, said enough.

Short Story · Literary Fiction · 2026

The Last Ordinary Day

A seemingly unremarkable day takes on a different meaning when its characters realize they will never experience it in quite the same way again.

The morning began the way every morning began in that house: the kettle first, then the radio, then the particular argument about whether the windows should be open or closed. Nobody in the family would later be able to say what was said at breakfast. It hadn't seemed worth remembering at the time.

By midday, the mother had hung the washing in the same order she always hung it — sheets first, along the outer line, so the smaller things could dry in their shade. The father had gone to the shop and come back with the wrong brand of tea, which prompted a complaint that had been made, in one form or another, for eleven years.

It was an ordinary day. That was, in the end, the whole of its significance.

In the evening, the youngest daughter noticed her father leave his cup on the veranda railing instead of carrying it inside, a small carelessness so unlike him that she almost said something. She didn't. There was nothing, that evening, that seemed to require comment.

They would not know, for another three weeks, that this had been the last evening the five of them sat in that courtyard together, in that configuration, in that house. A transfer letter would arrive. A hospital would call. A decision, already made somewhere out of sight, would begin to unfold in ways none of them could have read into the tea, the washing, the cup left carelessly on a railing.

Years later, the daughter would try to reconstruct that day in detail, the way you press on a bruise to see if it still hurts. She could remember the smell of the wrong tea. She could not remember what anyone had said. It occurred to her, finally, that this was the nature of the last ordinary day — it never announces itself. It only waits, patiently, to be recognized afterward, by people who were too busy living it to notice it was the one that mattered.

Short Story · Family Fiction · 2025

The House We Sold

Returning to a childhood home after years away, a daughter confronts the difference between the house she remembers and the place that remains.

She had expected the drive to take longer than it did. Childhood distances, it turned out, were mostly a matter of scale — the town had not grown, she had.

The new owners were kind enough to let her walk through. They had painted the walls a color her mother would have hated and moved the kitchen table to where the bookshelf used to stand. Still, she recognized the house immediately, the way you recognize a voice on the phone before the person says their name.

In the room that had been hers, a boy's bicycle leaned against the wall where her bed used to be. She stood there longer than was polite, trying to locate the exact spot where she'd once measured her height in pencil marks — painted over now, of course, along with everything else.

The courtyard felt smaller than she remembered, which she'd been warned about but hadn't believed. Here was where her grandmother had shelled peas in the evenings. Here was where her brother had broken his arm falling from the wall he'd been told, repeatedly, not to climb.

None of it belonged to her anymore. That was the strange part — not that the house had changed, but that it no longer needed her permission to change. It had a life of its own now, one she wasn't in.

Driving away, she understood something she hadn't been able to name before: the house she remembered and the house that stood on that street were, in fact, two different buildings occupying the same coordinates. One could be sold. The other, it turned out, could not — it had simply moved somewhere she could still visit, but never return to.

Short Story · Childhood Fiction · 2025

The Lake Has No Bottom

A child's mysterious belief about a lake gradually becomes a story about imagination, fear, and the loss of childhood certainty.

Every child in the village learned about the lake before they learned to swim in it. The older children were specific: nobody had ever touched the bottom. Divers had tried, ropes had been lowered, and still no one had found where it ended.

The adults offered explanations — silt, cold currents, an old irrigation channel that confused people's sense of depth — but explanations were no match for a good story, and the lake's mystery had a long head start.

For a while, the boy believed all of it. He imagined a second village beneath the surface, houses with their doors still open, waiting for people who had drowned generations ago and simply kept living down there, quietly, the way people do. He imagined creatures with too many eyes, patient enough to wait a hundred years for someone careless.

He was eleven when his cousin, visiting from the city and unimpressed by local mythology, waded out one afternoon and touched bottom in under four feet of water, not thirty yards from shore.

It should have ended the mystery. Instead, it complicated it. The boy went home unsettled, not because the lake had been explained, but because it had been explained so easily, by someone who hadn't even wanted to know.

He still remembers standing at the edge of that ordinary, shallow water, feeling something he didn't yet have the words for — the particular disappointment of growing older, in which every mystery, sooner or later, turns out to be something you could have waded into all along.

Short Story · Literary Fiction · 2025

The Mountain Behind the Bus Window

A passing view from a bus window becomes an unexpected landmark in the memory of a traveler.

The bus had been travelling for six hours when the mountain appeared. Most of the other passengers were asleep, or pretending to be, which is its own kind of sleep on long journeys.

He had been watching the landscape idly, the way you watch things you don't expect to remember — fields, a river, a line of electricity poles marching toward a horizon that never seemed to get closer. Then the road curved, and for perhaps ninety seconds, a mountain stood directly ahead of the bus, blue-grey, its upper half lost in cloud, close enough to seem enormous and far enough to seem unreal.

He didn't take a photograph. His phone was in his bag, and by the time he considered reaching for it, the road had curved again and the mountain was gone, folded back behind the hills that had been hiding it all along.

He never learned its name. He never returned to that road. And yet, years later, living in a city with no mountains at all, he would find himself thinking of it more often than places he had lived in for a decade — the specific blue of it, the way it had simply been there, uninterested in whether anyone was looking.

He came to think that memory doesn't reward effort so much as suddenness. The places he'd tried hardest to preserve — with photographs, with souvenirs, with deliberate goodbyes — had faded anyway. The mountain, which had asked nothing of him, refused to leave.

Short Story · Family Fiction · 2024

My Father's Postings

A child's memories of repeatedly leaving home reveal the quiet emotional cost of a family's constantly changing addresses.

By the time she was twelve, she had lived in five houses in four cities, and had developed the specific skill of making friends quickly and losing them without visible damage. It was, her mother said, simply what happened to a family that followed a father's postings.

Each new house had its own smell for the first week — paint, or dust, or someone else's cooking still lodged in the walls — before it settled into the ordinary smell of home. Each new school had its own version of the same first day: the teacher's introduction, the classroom's collective stare, the long walk to a seat near the back.

She began, without quite deciding to, collecting small things instead of people — a particular tree outside one school, a neighbor's voice that carried through a shared wall, the exact creak of a gate in a house she'd lived in for fourteen months. These were the things that didn't leave when she did, because she carried them herself.

Her father apologized once, on the drive to yet another new house, for what the moving had cost them. She told him, honestly, that she didn't mind — and mostly, this was true. What she didn't tell him was that she had stopped expecting home to be a place at all. Home, for her, had quietly become a method: notice quickly, attach carefully, remember generously.

It was not the childhood other people had. But she suspected, watching her own children grow up in one house, on one street, that she had gained something they might never need to learn — how to leave, and how to keep the leaving from being loss.

Short Story · Memory · 2024

The Photograph I Don't Have

The absence of a photograph leads a woman to question how much of a family history can survive without being recorded.

The photograph came up at every family gathering, always described in more detail than the last time. Her aunt remembered the exact arrangement — who stood where, who sat, who had been made to move at the last second because the light was wrong. Her uncle remembered the clothes, down to the color of a shawl no one else recalled seeing. Her mother remembered, above all, that her own grandmother had been smiling in it, which mattered to her more than anything else in the frame.

No one had the photograph. It had been lost, or lent, or possibly never developed — the story of its disappearance had almost as many versions as the story of its contents.

She had grown up believing she remembered it too, until one afternoon she realized, with some discomfort, that she couldn't actually picture her great-grandmother's face at all. What she had was a photograph of a photograph — an image built entirely from other people's descriptions, repeated so often it had come to feel like memory.

This unsettled her more than she expected. If a memory could be manufactured this convincingly from nothing but retelling, how much of the rest of her family's history was built the same way — sincere, detailed, and entirely secondhand?

She stopped asking about the photograph after that, not because she'd lost interest, but because she'd begun to suspect that the photograph's real value had never been in what it showed. It was in what it had given the family permission to imagine together, for thirty years, in its absence.

Short Story · Family Fiction · 2024

When the Lights Went Out

During an unexpected power outage, a family temporarily steps away from their screens and rediscovers the conversations they had forgotten how to have.

The outage lasted four hours, which was unremarkable by the standards of that particular summer. What was remarkable was what happened inside the house during it.

For the first twenty minutes, everyone simply waited, the way people wait for a delayed film to resume — phones held up hopefully, half-charged, useless without a signal worth using. The children complained. The father checked his phone out of habit, twice, before remembering there was nothing to check.

Then the grandmother, seated by the window for the breeze, began telling a story about her own childhood that none of them had heard before — a flood, a lost dog, an uncle who had once outrun a wild boar and never let anyone forget it. One story invited another. The mother remembered an incident from her wedding that made everyone laugh in a way the family hadn't laughed together in months.

By the time the electricity returned, no one moved to switch anything back on immediately. The room sat for a moment in the new, humming light, as if deciding whether it wanted it.

Later, the father would half-joke that they should turn the power off on purpose, once a month, just to see what else they'd forgotten they had. No one took him up on it. But for a while afterward, dinner lasted a little longer than usual, and someone always seemed to have one more story left to tell.

Short Story · Place & Landscape · 2023

The Salt Road

A journey through the Salt Range becomes an encounter with stories, landscapes, and histories hidden beneath an ordinary road.

The road through the Salt Range had never struck him as anything more than a route — a way of getting from one ordinary place to another, distinguished mostly by its potholes and the heat that pressed down on it by midday.

It was the driver, an older man who had made the same trip for thirty years, who first mentioned the shrine half-buried near the third bend, and the well beyond it that no longer held water but had, apparently, once served an entire caravan route. He spoke of it the way people speak of things they've stopped finding remarkable — factually, without embellishment, the way you'd mention a landmark on a road you no longer really see.

At a tea stall further along, an old man added more: a story of a settlement that had once stood where there was now only a flat stretch of scrubland, abandoned after a drought two generations back. Nothing marked the place. No sign, no ruin. Only the story, passed from one driver, one tea stall, to the next.

By the end of the journey, the road had stopped feeling like a road at all. It felt more like a sentence someone had been writing for centuries, one traveler's memory added to the next, none of it recorded anywhere but in the retelling.

He has driven that road many times since. He no longer sees it as a route between two points. He sees it as something closer to a ledger — of settlements, of droughts, of caravans, of ordinary people whose only monument is a story still being told at a tea stall, to whoever happens to be passing through.

Short Story · Literary Fiction · 2023

The House That Remembered

Told through the presence of an old family house, the story follows generations of departures, returns, celebrations, and loss.

The house had outlived three generations by the time it stood empty. It had seen a wedding held in its courtyard under a canopy that no longer exists, a birth attended by a midwife whose name only the eldest living relative could still recall, and a funeral so large the street outside had to be closed for the afternoon.

A pencil mark on the kitchen doorframe recorded a child's height at seven, at nine, at eleven, and then stopped — the child had grown up and moved to the city, as children in that family generally did. A crack in the courtyard wall, patched twice, still ran in roughly the same place it always had, indifferent to whoever had tried to erase it.

By the time the last of the family left, the house had become mostly quiet — not empty, exactly, but reduced to holding what could no longer be added to. The furniture went first, then the smaller things, until only the walls remained to do the remembering.

A cousin, visiting years later before the sale was finalized, walked through each room slowly, running a hand along the same doorframe, the same wall. She couldn't have said what she was looking for. Perhaps only confirmation that the house had, in fact, held what she remembered — that it hadn't simply imagined a family, the way a family sometimes imagines a house.

It had. The marks were still there, faint but legible, in a language only the family had ever really spoken.

Short Story · Technology & Human Life · 2023

The Signal

In a world where everyone is constantly connected, a broken signal forces one person to confront a loneliness that technology cannot solve.

She had over three hundred contacts and rarely felt she had anyone to call. The apartment stayed lit blue most evenings, notifications arriving in a steady, reassuring rhythm that she had come to mistake, without quite noticing, for company.

The outage, when it came, lasted only six hours — a fault at the local exchange, the message said later, apologetically. For the first hour, she found herself picking up her phone out of habit, an unconscious twitch toward a screen that had nothing to offer her.

By the second hour, restless, she stepped out onto the landing, where she found a neighbor doing much the same thing — leaning against the railing, looking, for lack of anything better to look at, at the street below.

They had lived on the same floor for two years and exchanged, in that time, perhaps a dozen words. That evening, with nothing else competing for their attention, they talked for nearly an hour — about nothing important, about the heat, about a stray cat that had adopted the stairwell. It was, she realized afterward, the longest conversation she'd had with an actual, physically present person in longer than she wanted to admit.

When the signal returned, her phone buzzed insistently, three hours of notifications arriving all at once. She looked at it for a moment, then set it face-down on the railing and stayed outside a while longer, talking to the one person, that evening, who hadn't required a signal at all.

The Geography of Silence Poetry Collection

The Geography of Silence

Poetry Collection · Completed

A quiet collection tracing the spaces between words — grief, stillness, and the landscapes that hold what we cannot say aloud.

About the book & contents

Genre: Poetry · Year: 2026 · Themes: Silence, Memory, Nature, Childhood, Solitude, Family, Belonging

The Geography of Silence is a poetry collection concerned with the spaces that exist beyond spoken language. Its poems explore silence not as emptiness, but as a landscape filled with memory, emotion, absence, observation, and things left unsaid.

The collection moves through familiar landscapes—quiet roads, trees, evening skies, old houses, lakes, fields, and mountains—using them as emotional maps. Childhood memories appear alongside reflections on family, distance, change, and the passage of time.

The poems ask how much a person can communicate without speaking and how much a landscape can reveal without having a voice. Silence becomes a language through which memory survives.

Where the Salt Hills Remember Literary Collection

Where the Salt Hills Remember

About the book & contents

Genre: Literary Nonfiction / Nature Writing · Year: 2026 · Themes: Salt Range, Landscape, Memory, Family, Childhood, Heritage, Place

Where the Salt Hills Remember is rooted in the landscapes of the Salt Range and the intimate relationship between people and place.

The collection explores mountains, lakes, fields, village roads, trees, family homes, changing seasons, and ordinary moments of rural life. These landscapes are not presented simply as scenery. They become witnesses to childhood, family histories, traditions, departures, returns, and the gradual transformation of communities.

The book asks what a landscape can preserve. Mountains may remain while generations change. Roads may be rebuilt while memories remain. Fields may disappear beneath new development while the people who once knew them continue to remember them.

Through literary observation and personal reflection, the collection considers the Salt Range as both a physical geography and an emotional one.

The Lake and the Circuit Poetry · Nonfiction · Nature Writing

The Lake and the Circuit

Poetry · Literary Nonfiction · Nature Writing · Current / Ongoing

An evolving collection at the meeting point of nature and technology — how digital life is quietly reshaping home and belonging.

About the book & contents

Genre: Literary Nonfiction / Hybrid Writing · Year: 2026 · Themes: Nature, Technology, Identity, Memory, Tradition, Modernity

The Lake and the Circuit explores two landscapes that appear fundamentally different: the natural landscape of lakes, hills, fields, and memory, and the technological landscape of computers, circuits, networks, and digital life.

The project emerges from the tension between these two worlds. One represents inherited landscapes and physical experience; the other represents technological change and the increasingly digital nature of modern life.

The collection asks whether these worlds must remain separate. It considers how technology changes our understanding of home, communication, memory, work, and even nature itself.

Through essays and poetic reflections, the book brings together the natural and technological worlds to examine what happens when a person grows up among landscapes of stone and water while simultaneously entering a world shaped by screens, code, machines, and digital networks.

  • Part II — The CircuitThe Circuit, Inside the Machine, A World of Screens, The Language of Code, Digital Memory
  • Part III — Between Two LandscapesBetween Tradition and Technology, The Old Road and the New Network, Nature and the Machine, Two Ways of Remembering, The Human Between Worlds

  • Part V — ReconciliationThe Lake and the Circuit, A Different Kind of Landscape, Beyond the Binary, Returning to the Physical World, Two Landscapes, One Life

The project concludes by suggesting that technology and nature do not have to be opposing forces. The challenge is to remain connected to the physical world while navigating the increasingly digital one.

A Voice Between Two Landscapes Literary Essays

A Voice Between Two Landscapes

Literary Essays / Creative Nonfiction · Completed

Essays reading a single place through two prisms — the hillside and the hard drive — and the spaces where they overlap.

About the book & contents

Genre: Literary Essays / Creative Nonfiction · Year: 2026 · Themes: Place, Nature, Technology, Tradition, Memory, Identity, Modernity

A Voice Between Two Landscapes is a collection of literary essays that reads a single place through two prisms: the hillside and the hard drive.

The collection explores the experience of growing up within a physical landscape shaped by mountains, lakes, family histories, traditions, and rural surroundings while simultaneously entering a technological world shaped by computers, digital communication, networks, and rapid change.

The two landscapes are not presented as opposites. Instead, the book explores the spaces where they overlap. A childhood memory can exist alongside a digital photograph. A traditional story can travel through a modern device. A family home can become connected to people who live thousands of miles away.

The essays therefore explore a central question: how can a person remain connected to an inherited sense of place while becoming part of an increasingly technological world?

  • Part I — The HillsideThe Landscape I Inherited, The Hills Beyond Home, A Childhood Among Hills, The Language of Stone, The Places That Raised Us
  • Part II — The Hard DriveEntering the Digital World, The First Screen, Memory in Machines, The Architecture of Technology, A Life Connected
  • Part III — TraditionThe Stories We Inherit, The Silence Between Generations, Family Traditions, What Modernity Changes, The Things Worth Keeping
  • Part IV — TechnologyBetween Tradition and Technology, When Technology Changes the Meaning of Home, Digital Distance, Living Through Screens, The New Geography of Connection
  • Part V — Between Two LandscapesA Voice Between Two Landscapes, The Lake and the Circuit, Where Nature Meets Technology, What We Carry Forward, A Future With Memory

The collection ends with neither landscape rejecting the other. Instead, it asks whether identity can be built from both—the physical places that shape our earliest memories and the technological spaces that increasingly shape our future.

Author's Note

My writing begins with place.

I am interested in the landscapes that surround ordinary lives and in the memories that become attached to them. Mountains, lakes, fields, trees, family homes, roads, and changing villages often appear in my work because they are not merely geographical features. They are part of how people remember.

At the same time, I write from within a technological generation. Computers, digital communication, networks, and modern technology have become part of everyday experience. This creates a space between two worlds that I continue to explore in my writing.

My books move through this space between landscape and memory, tradition and technology, childhood and adulthood, permanence and change.

I write to preserve what may otherwise become invisible: the emotional history of a place, the quiet details of family life, and the memories carried by landscapes as they change.

Leadership philosophy

"Leadership, where I come from, looks less like standing in front of people and more like staying beside them until they trust their own voice."

I believe leadership is mostly attention: noticing who has gone quiet, who is struggling, who is nearly ready to lead something themselves. The study circles and mentoring I have run were never about my expertise — they worked because students taught each other and discovered they were capable. I want to keep building rooms like that, in universities, in communities, and on the page.
